lesson.title: The Discomfort of Contradiction: Cognitive Dissonance
lesson.summary: Cognitive dissonance is the uncomfortable mental tension that arises when a person holds two conflicting beliefs, or acts in a way that conflicts with their own attitudes or self image, and it motivates people to reduce that discomfort, often by changing what they believe rather than what they did.
lesson.body:
Cognitive dissonance theory, developed by Leon Festinger in the late 1950s, starts from a simple premise: people are motivated to feel that their thoughts, attitudes, and actions are consistent with one another. When two cognitions clash, for example "I am a careful, honest person" and "I just told a convenient lie," the resulting tension is genuinely unpleasant, not just intellectually inconsistent but emotionally uncomfortable. Because that discomfort is aversive, people are driven to reduce it, and they can do so in a few different ways: by changing the belief, changing the behavior, adding a new justifying belief, or minimizing the importance of the conflict altogether.

This idea connects directly to attribution theory, the study of how people explain the causes of behavior. Dissonance reduction is essentially a special case of self attribution under pressure: when our actions do not match our attitudes, we often resolve the discomfort not by admitting we acted against our values, but by quietly revising our account of why we acted, or even revising the attitude itself so that the behavior no longer looks inconsistent. It is also a clear illustration of how cognitive biases in general are not random errors. They are often the predictable byproduct of a mind trying to protect a coherent sense of self.

The classic demonstration comes from a study by Festinger and James Carlsmith in 1959. Participants completed a deliberately boring task and were then asked to tell the next participant, waiting in the hallway, that the task had actually been interesting. Some participants were paid one dollar for this small lie, others were paid twenty dollars. Afterward, when asked to rate how enjoyable the original task really was, the participants paid only one dollar rated it as significantly more enjoyable than the participants paid twenty dollars did. This result seems backward at first, since more money should produce more attitude change, not less, but dissonance theory explains it well: the twenty dollar participants had ample external justification for lying, so they felt little internal tension and did not need to change their attitude. The one dollar participants had very little external justification, so to resolve the dissonance between "I lied" and "I am not the kind of person who lies for no good reason," many of them unconsciously convinced themselves that the task had actually been somewhat enjoyable after all.

Cognitive dissonance shows up constantly in everyday decision making. After making a difficult choice between two similarly attractive options, people often experience post decision dissonance and respond by emphasizing the positives of the option they chose while downplaying the option they gave up, a pattern sometimes called effort justification when it follows painful or costly initiation into a group. The more a person suffers to join something, the more they tend to value it afterward, because valuing it less would leave the suffering unexplained. This drive to protect existing beliefs, rather than update them cleanly in light of new information, is also the seed of the next concept, belief perseverance.
